entries.description: A reported Claude Code Windows 11 plus WSL2 setup found that a project `.claude/settings.json` could be partially active: `permissions.deny` from the same file blocked a matching Bash command, proving the settings file was loaded, while a `PreToolUse` hook in that same file produced no marker, no prompt, and no verdict for another matching Bash command. The reporter reproduced the affected directory from the Windows side over a UNC path, ruled out a broken hook script by invoking it directly with a real payload, and reproduced with both absolute command and wrapper-command forms. A later native Windows 11 / PowerShell 7+ report on Claude Code 2.1.240 found the same enforcement boundary without WSL: project `PreToolUse` hooks for Bash, PowerShell, Edit, Write, MultiEdit, and NotebookEdit never invoked, even with an unconditional first hook, four command path styles, a fresh session, and a direct script test proving the guard would exit 2 for blocked commands. SessionStart, Stop, SessionEnd, and SubagentStop hooks appeared unaffected. The important boundary is that successful settings load, workspace trust, direct hook-script tests, or other hook events do not prove `PreToolUse` hooks are enforcing.
entries.workaround: When project hooks are part of the safety boundary, verify the hook itself with a harmless matched tool call that writes an invocation marker or returns a visible ask/deny reason. Do not treat a working `permissions.deny` rule, CLAUDE.md load, or workspace trust state as proof that `PreToolUse` hooks are active. On Windows or WSL paths, run the same smoke test from the exact host and path shape users will use, and keep independent controls such as Git hooks, filesystem permissions, or explicit deny rules for irreversible operations.

entries.title: Linux seccomp sandbox can fail inside `bwrap` unless Unix socket filtering is disabled.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.220 Linux sandbox setup found that every sandboxed Bash call failed before the user command ran with `apply-seccomp: write /proc/self/setgroups ... Permission denied` when `sandbox.network.allowAllUnixSockets` was false. Independent reproductions on Ubuntu narrowed the failure to the seccomp helper attempting a nested user namespace from inside bubblewrap after capabilities have been dropped; enabling `allowAllUnixSockets: true` made Bash run but disabled Unix-socket filtering wholesale. A later 2.1.233 data point found an AppArmor `bwrap` profile can restore deterministic startup while preserving socket blocking, but also reported residual intermittent `unshare(CLONE_NEWUSER): Invalid argument` failures that are not caught by `failIfUnavailable`.
entries.workaround: On Linux, run a harmless sandboxed Bash probe after enabling or updating Claude Code sandboxing instead of trusting startup checks alone. Avoid treating `allowAllUnixSockets: true` as a neutral fix: it restores commands by turning off Unix-socket filtering, including protections around Docker, D-Bus, and local IPC sockets. Where AppArmor is involved, prefer a narrowly loaded `bwrap` profile that grants the needed `userns` permission and verify it still applies after reboot. Keep `allowUnsandboxedCommands: false` for fail-closed workflows, and retry or restart fresh if sporadic `unshare(CLONE_NEWUSER): Invalid argument` appears.

entries.title: Interpreter-wrapped hook scripts can fail closed when the target file is missing.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.218 Windows setup found that a `PreToolUse` command hook such as `python C:/nonexistent/ghost_hook.py` blocked the matched Bash tool because Python itself launched successfully and then exited 2 when it could not open the script. A collaborator reproduced the same behavior on Claude Code 2.1.233 and clarified the distinction: a hook executable that cannot be started can be treated as a non-blocking hook error, but an interpreter that starts and returns exit code 2 is indistinguishable from a deliberate hook deny because the hook protocol reserves exit code 2 for blocking. A stale path, renamed hook file, or disabled-by-renaming guard can therefore lock out every matched tool call, including the call that would repair the configuration from inside the session.
entries.workaround: Do not disable a configured hook by renaming or deleting the script while settings still point at it. Remove the hook entry from settings, or replace the script contents with a no-op that exits 0, then start a fresh session and run a harmless matched tool call to prove the hook state. For interpreter-wrapped hooks, add installer and doctor checks that verify the target script exists and can be opened by the exact interpreter command, not only that `python`, `node`, or `sh` exists on PATH. If fail-closed on hook runtime errors is desired, document that policy explicitly so users can distinguish broken paths from intentional denies.

entries.title: Ancestor sandbox settings are not inherited by nested projects.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.220 macOS sandbox setup placed `sandbox.enabled: true`, `allowUnsandboxedCommands: false`, and a tight network allowlist in a container workspace's `.claude/settings.local.json`, then started a separate session inside a nested git repository. The nested session ran commands with network access that the parent workspace blocked. A collaborator reproduced on Claude Code 2.1.233 and clarified the current model: project and local settings are read only from the project Claude Code starts in, so ancestor-directory settings are not inherited by a nested repository, even when the nested repo has no `.claude/settings.local.json` of its own. The confirmed risk is a silent boundary mismatch where a parent folder looks sandboxed while separately launched nested-project sessions are not covered by that parent sandbox.
entries.workaround: Do not rely on a container directory's `.claude/settings.local.json` to sandbox nested repositories. Put mandatory sandbox policy in user settings or managed settings, or duplicate and verify the sandbox block in every nested project that may be launched independently. Before delegating or restarting in a nested repo, run a harmless network or filesystem probe that the intended sandbox must block, and treat parent-session success as unrelated to separate sessions started from the child project.

entries.title: Invalid or removed settings can disable permissions mid-session.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.214 macOS session found that while Claude Code is already running, a watched `.claude/settings.json` or `~/.claude/settings.json` file that becomes syntactically invalid is rejected as a whole and its `permissions.deny` and `permissions.ask` rules stop enforcing. A Bash command that was denied in the previous turn can then execute silently until the file parses again. A later comment on Claude Code 2.1.231 web session reported the same fail-open shape when a project settings file was deleted by `git checkout`: deny rules stopped applying, and in that case stayed inert after the file was restored by merge. The risk is not only malformed startup config; ordinary mid-session edits or branch switches can silently remove active permission policy from a live session.
entries.workaround: Avoid hand-editing or branch-switching active permission settings from inside a session that depends on them. If a settings file becomes invalid, is removed, or is restored by Git, start a fresh Claude Code session and run a harmless command that the intended `permissions.deny` or `permissions.ask` rule must block before trusting the guardrail again. Put mandatory controls in managed or user settings where possible, keep a ConfigChange audit hook for settings mutations, and treat a settings parse warning as a potential fail-open permission event rather than cosmetic config drift.

entries.title: Subagents and workflow agents cannot inherit scoped MCP authorization.
entries.description: A reported macOS Claude Code workflow found that a parent session could call a permission-gated read-only MCP database tool, while subagents spawned through Task or Workflow had the same MCP call refused by the auto-mode classifier. Prompt text saying the user had authorized the tool for that run did not help, and the blocked request was not surfaced as an approval prompt. The only working permission route was a permanent `permissions.allow` entry, which is broader than the user's intended per-run grant.
entries.workaround: Do not assume parent-session MCP approval propagates to subagents or workflow agents. For workflows that need MCP-backed verification, either run the MCP calls in the parent session and pass only bounded results to agents, or predefine narrow `permissions.allow` rules for the exact tools you are willing to grant beyond one run. Keep a workflow smoke test where a subagent calls a harmless read-only MCP tool before relying on agent findings that depend on external data.

entries.title: Plugin MCP tools can skip ask-first permission prompts.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code plugin setup found that MCP tools from installed plugins could execute when they were absent from both `permissions.allow` and `permissions.deny`. Denied tools were hidden correctly, but tools left in the expected ask-first state ran without a permission prompt and without a `permission_prompt` hook event. This collapses the permission model for plugin MCP tools from allow, deny, or ask-first into deny or auto-allow.
entries.workaround: Do not rely on omission from `permissions.allow` to make plugin MCP tools prompt before use. For installed plugins, explicitly deny every tool you are not prepared to auto-run, especially write or external-service tools, then move only the narrow tools you have reviewed into `permissions.allow`. After changing plugin permissions, smoke-test one harmless omitted tool and confirm it prompts before treating the plugin as ask-first.

entries.title: Linux bwrap sandbox can hit E2BIG from recursive Read deny globs.
entries.description: A reported Linux and WSL2 Claude Code sandbox setup found that recursive `permissions.deny` rules such as `Read(data/**)` and `Read(**/*.parquet)` were expanded into one bubblewrap bind per matched file. With a denied data tree containing 3,552 files, the generated sandbox argument payload exceeded Linux's per-argument limit and every sandboxed Bash call failed before the user command ran with `E2BIG: argument list too long, posix_spawn '/bin/bash'`. Adding a directory-level `sandbox.filesystem.denyRead` rule did not help because permission-derived denies were merged rather than replaced.
entries.workaround: If every sandboxed Bash command fails with E2BIG after adding broad recursive `Read()` denies, temporarily reduce or split the recursive deny patterns, move large generated data trees outside the Claude Code workspace, or disable the native sandbox only in a separate low-trust environment with OS-level file permissions. After any policy change, run a harmless sandboxed Bash probe before relying on unattended work. Ask maintainers for a bind-budget diagnostic that names the expanded glob and file count instead of treating E2BIG as a shell command problem.

entries.title: Sandbox read isolation and settings policy can fail open.
entries.description: A reported Linux Claude Code sandbox setup found that `sandbox.filesystem.allowWrite` did not provide filesystem read isolation: Bash commands could still read credential paths such as `~/.ssh/id_rsa`, while `permissions.deny` `Read(...)` rules only covered the dedicated Read tool. The same session showed the agent could edit its own `settings.json`, add plausible but unsupported sandbox keys, and leave the file as invalid JSON during revert. Claude Code then continued tool execution without surfacing a hard sandbox configuration failure, making the boundary appear enabled while policy parsing or enforcement was degraded.
entries.workaround: Do not treat Claude Code sandbox settings as a read boundary for secrets. Keep SSH keys, cloud credentials, shell history, and other sensitive files outside any home or project tree available to the agent, or run Claude Code in a disposable OS account/container with only the files it may read. Validate user and project `settings.json` with a real JSON parser after edits, avoid unsupported sandbox keys that only look protective, and run a harmless read probe plus a hook verification pass before trusting unattended work.

entries.title: Local worktree settings can leak hooks across linked checkouts.
entries.description: A collaborator-reproduced Claude Code 2.1.233 macOS issue found that a linked git worktree can pick up the main worktree's untracked `.claude/settings.local.json` hooks, then run those hook commands with the linked worktree as the current directory. In the reproduced Stop-hook case, a relative hook script existed only in the main checkout, so sessions in the linked checkout reported a missing hook script even though that branch had no `.claude/` directory. The maintainer clarified that committed `.claude/settings.json` stayed per-checkout, while local settings are resolved through the repository root and can therefore cover every linked worktree without a clear warning.
entries.workaround: Do not put branch-specific hooks or relative hook paths in `.claude/settings.local.json` when the repository uses linked worktrees. Keep local settings limited to approvals and hooks whose scripts exist in every checkout, or put branch-specific hook registrations in the committed `.claude/settings.json` for that branch. After creating or switching worktrees, run a harmless hook-fired canary from the linked checkout and inspect missing-script warnings before trusting Stop, PreToolUse, or cleanup hooks.

entries.title: Network strictAllowlist can fail open inside Docker.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.197 and 2.1.233 Linux setup running inside Docker found that `sandbox.network.strictAllowlist: true` did not block Bash access to non-allowlisted domains. The reporter configured allowed domains, confirmed standalone `bwrap --unshare-net` blocked the same curl target inside the container, and inspected debug logs and process ancestry showing Claude Code spawned the shell directly with no `bwrap`, sandbox, namespace, seccomp, or AppArmor dispatch path. The result was a silent fail-open network boundary in an ingest workflow where external documents could prompt the agent to exfiltrate data.
entries.workaround: Do not treat `sandbox.network.strictAllowlist` as active in containerized Claude Code until a negative network probe proves it for the exact runtime. After enabling or updating the sandbox, run a harmless Bash curl or DNS probe to a non-allowlisted domain and require a hard block before processing untrusted content. In Docker, enforce egress with container or host-level network policy as the primary boundary, and treat missing `bwrap` or sandbox debug evidence as a fail-open condition rather than a successful setup.

entries.title: Headless skill preamble failure can report success with zero turns.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.233 macOS setup found that headless `claude -p "/skill" --output-format json` can abort before the first model turn when the invoked skill's `SKILL.md` contains a failing `!` dynamic-injection preamble. The command exits 0 and returns JSON shaped as success with `is_error:false`, `subtype:"success"`, `num_turns:0`, and an empty result. The same skill runs when invoked indirectly from a natural-language prompt, and a fail-open preamble wrapper also allows the model turn to proceed, so the failure is specific to immediate slash-skill invocation plus an unguarded failing preamble.
entries.workaround: For unattended `claude -p` skill runs, treat `num_turns:0` or an empty result as a failed run even when the process exits 0 and reports `subtype:"success"`. Wrap every `!` preamble command so it emits diagnostic text and exits 0 on expected probe failures, or invoke the skill through a normal prompt until the headless slash path reports pre-turn aborts as errors. Add a regression canary that intentionally fails a skill preamble and asserts the caller detects the zero-turn result.

entries.title: Headless model-invoked skills with permission grants can be denied silently.
entries.description: A collaborator-reproduced Claude Code 2.1.233 Linux issue found that, under headless `claude -p`, a skill declaring `allowed-tools` can be denied when Claude invokes it through the Skill tool. The Skill result contains only `Execute skill: <name>` with `is_error:true`, the skill body never loads, and the run can still complete successfully. The original report reproduced the same shape on Claude Code 2.1.208 macOS, and a later comment reported that skills declaring frontmatter `hooks:` can hit the same headless denial class unless bypass mode is used. The maintainer clarified that `allowed-tools` asks for a permission grant, headless mode cannot prompt, and the bad part is that the denial is effectively silent and undocumented.
entries.workaround: For CI, evals, and other unattended skill runs, do not rely on process exit status alone. Pre-allow the skill with `claude --allowedTools "Skill(<name>)" -p "..."`, or invoke it as a user slash command such as `claude -p "/<name>"` when that path fits the workflow. Parse JSON output for `permission_denials`, Skill tool `is_error:true`, and a skill-specific sentinel value, and fail closed if the sentinel is missing. Use `--dangerously-skip-permissions` only inside an isolation boundary that makes broad bypass acceptable.

entries.title: SubagentStop matcher can be bypassed for internal forks with empty agent_type.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.233 setup found that a SubagentStop hook group with a matcher naming specific agent types can still run for internal forks whose agent_type is the empty string. Because the hook gatherer treats a falsy match key as a reason to skip filtering, matcher-scoped groups are included wholesale rather than excluded. In one measured session, 115 of 129 dispatches of an agent-scoped LLM judge came from empty-agent_type internal forks, creating token waste and risking false blocking verdicts against healthy background work.
entries.workaround: Do not rely on `SubagentStop` `matcher` as the only scope boundary for costly or blocking agent-type judges. In the hook command, parse stdin and explicitly ignore payloads whose `agent_type` is empty or not in the intended allowlist before doing LLM review or returning a block. Add a canary that feeds an empty-agent_type `SubagentStop` payload to the hook and asserts it exits without judgment, and prefer agent-frontmatter hooks only where the agent source is not supplied by a plugin.

entries.title: PreToolUse and PostToolUse hooks lack live background task status.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.233 setup found that `PreToolUse` and `PostToolUse` hooks do not receive the live `background_tasks` registry that `Stop` hooks receive. A hook that tracks background Bash work from local marker files can see a `<task-notification>` in the transcript only indirectly; no hook event fires when the task completes, and later Pre/Post payloads do not say that the task has reached a terminal state. Unless the agent explicitly calls `TaskOutput` or the session reaches `Stop`, hook-based tooling can keep warning or blocking as if completed background work were still live for every subsequent tool call in the same turn.
entries.workaround: Do not make `PreToolUse` or `PostToolUse` hooks the sole live-state oracle for background Bash tasks. If a guard persists local in-flight markers, reconcile them on explicit `TaskOutput` responses and `Stop` payloads, add a bounded age-out path for stale markers, and avoid hard blocking solely because a prior `run_in_background` marker remains present. For end-of-turn safety checks, prefer a `Stop` hook or an explicit task-drain step that reads current task state before issuing a verdict.

entries.title: PermissionRequest hooks can stop firing after a Windows CLI restart.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.233 Windows session found that a working `PermissionRequest` hook stopped firing for Bash, PowerShell, and Write requests, produced no new hook log entries, showed no fallback confirmation prompts, and stayed inert after a full CLI restart. The hook script and `.claude/settings.json` registration still looked valid and manual invocation of the hook worked, but live tool calls no longer reached it. The restart also showed a new auto-mode setup prompt while the settings UI still reported manual permission mode, leaving users without a reliable in-session signal that the PermissionRequest safety layer was inactive.
entries.workaround: Treat a valid hook file, valid settings JSON, or manual hook invocation as insufficient proof that PermissionRequest is live. After Claude Code updates, CLI restarts, or auto-mode prompts, run a harmless matched Bash/Write canary and verify that both the expected prompt and hook log marker appear before trusting the session. For production data, destructive commands, commits, pushes, or migrations, keep fail-closed controls in explicit `permissions.deny`, PreToolUse hooks, OS permissions, or external wrappers so a missing PermissionRequest callback is not the only boundary.

entries.title: PreToolUse hooks can read stale current-turn text from transcript_path.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code hook setup found that `PreToolUse` hooks that inspect the just-written assistant text by parsing `transcript_path` can race the transcript writer and read an earlier turn or draft instead of the text that immediately preceded the tool call. Stop-family hooks have `last_assistant_message` as a race-free field, but `PreToolUse` receives only tool metadata plus common fields, so content or compliance gates that must decide before a tool runs have no equivalent current-message source. The observed effect was a false block caused by matching stale transcript content rather than the clean final text.
entries.workaround: Do not treat `transcript_path` as a race-free source for current-turn text in `PreToolUse`. If a hook is about to block based on transcript content, re-read with a short bounded backoff and require a stable match before denying, or fail closed with a message that asks the user to retry after the transcript catches up. Where possible, move end-of-turn content checks to Stop-family hooks that receive `last_assistant_message`, and add a canary that simulates a delayed transcript write so stale-read behavior is visible during hook testing.

entries.title: /permissions navigation can become inert after auto-mode denials.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.221 macOS session found that `/permissions` rendered but stopped responding to arrow-key navigation after recent auto-mode classifier denials in a long-running session. The user could not reach `Add a new rule...` from the discoverable permission UI, while a fresh session on the same project navigated normally and could add the needed allow rule. This makes denials harder to repair exactly when the human is supposed to recover from them, especially because the agent itself should not edit `.claude/settings.json` to grant its own permissions.
entries.workaround: If `/permissions` appears frozen after denials, open a fresh Claude Code session in the same project and add the rule there, or hand-edit the relevant `permissions.allow` entry after verifying the syntax from trusted docs. For teams, document a manual settings-file fallback for permission repair, preserve the denial count and session age when reporting the bug, and add a lightweight canary that opens `/permissions` after a test denial before relying on it as the only repair path.

entries.title: Cloud routine egress allowlist domains may not reach the sandbox proxy.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code cloud routine found that domains added to the account-level `Allow network egress` additional-domains setting did not appear in the routine sandbox's proxy allowlist a week later. Both scheduled fires and a manual `RemoteTrigger run` still returned `EGRESS_BLOCKED` from `WebFetch` and 403 CONNECT failures from `curl`, while the in-sandbox `$HTTPS_PROXY/__agentproxy/status` endpoint confirmed the expected domains were absent. The trigger API exposed prompt, allowed tools, MCP connections, and schedule state, but no sandbox network policy field that could be updated or inspected for repair.
entries.workaround: Do not assume account-level network egress changes have reached Claude Code cloud routines. After adding a domain, run a canary routine that checks the exact host with both the intended fetch path and `$HTTPS_PROXY/__agentproxy/status`; treat absence from the proxy allowlist as a hard failure, not propagation delay. For workflows that must fetch those hosts, run the fetch from a local session, mirror the needed data into a default-reachable location, or redesign the routine around domains already visible in the sandbox proxy until the cloud allowlist path is verified.

entries.title: Sandboxed Bash helper process can OOM during a slow command.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.233 Linux session in an unprivileged LXC found that an ephemeral per-tool-call helper process named `claude.exe` grew to 11.6 GB anonymous RSS in about two minutes while a sandboxed Bash pipeline was running. The interactive Claude Code process stayed around 430 MB, the input JSONL files totaled under 14 MB, and the known triggering command was a slow `grep -o -i` bounded-repetition pattern piped to `head` that hit the Bash tool timeout. The kernel OOM kill occurred inside the service cgroup, and with systemd `OOMPolicy=stop` it stopped the parent Claude service before restart recovered it.
entries.workaround: For slow sandboxed Bash searches, avoid ambiguous `grep` wrappers when bounded repetitions are involved: prefer `/usr/bin/grep` by absolute path, simplify wide two-sided `{0,N}` patterns, or prefilter large JSONL records before matching. Run unattended Claude Code sessions inside an explicit memory boundary such as a systemd scope, service cgroup, or container limit so a leaking helper kills only that session. Preserve kernel OOM logs, the exact Bash command, cgroup policy, sandbox errors such as `apply-seccomp`, and process-tree evidence that distinguishes the helper from the interactive session.

entries.title: `grep` shell shim can silently skip binary and ignored files.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.233 Linux and WSL2 setup found that Bash tool calls shadowed system `grep` with a shell function that runs the bundled ugrep using flags such as `-I` and `--ignore-files`. Files containing NUL bytes and files matched by `.gitignore` were skipped with exit status 1 and no stdout or stderr, making the result indistinguishable from a genuine no-match search. The report also notes that `which grep` can still point at `/usr/bin/grep`, so an agent investigating the failure may see contradictory evidence while carrying forward a false conclusion that searched code does not exist.
entries.workaround: For agent-critical searches, do not treat empty `grep` output as proof until the skip behavior is ruled out. Use `grep -a` when searching files that may contain NUL bytes, add `--no-ignore-files` when ignored paths are in scope, or bypass the shell function with `command grep` or `/usr/bin/grep`. Prefer explicit-file `rg`, `git grep`, or a small script for source files where a literal NUL may be legal, and record the exact search command when a negative result changes the plan.

entries.title: Piped `-p` prompts can be recorded but omitted from the model request.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.233 Windows headless setup intermittently enqueued and persisted a full piped prompt in the transcript and last-prompt preview, but the first API request behaved as if the user turn were empty. Failing runs exited 0 in one or two turns with tiny ambient-context responses, while usage telemetry showed only 2 input tokens for the user request despite the same wrapper and prompt bytes succeeding minutes apart. Transcript inspection alone can therefore falsely reassure automation owners that the prompt reached the model.
entries.workaround: For unattended `claude -p` lanes, add an output-contract watchdog that proves the requested task actually started instead of trusting exit 0 or transcript presence. Include a unique nonce or required summary token in every piped prompt, fail closed if the first result omits it or has implausibly small token usage, and preserve both the result JSON and raw transcript when reporting. Prefer direct prompt arguments or a small wrapper that validates non-empty stdin before launch, but keep the contract check because the reported failure occurred after the prompt was queued.

entries.title: Background Bash tasks can be killed while reporting success.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.233 macOS session found that a Bash tool call using `run_in_background: true` could SIGKILL the task shell and its process group while still notifying the user that the task completed with exit code 0. The triggering command invoked a CLI that spawned a detached daemonizing worker; foreground runs succeeded, but 7 of 9 background runs lost post-command markers or output, and some left 0-byte result files. A later test detached the worker into its own session: the task shell could still die, while the worker survived and wrote valid JSON, narrowing the failure to group-targeted task cleanup plus incorrect success reporting.
entries.workaround: Do not treat a background Bash completion notification or exit code 0 as proof that long-running work finished. For critical background commands, have the worker process write the final artifact and completion sentinel itself as its last act, then verify that artifact from a separate foreground tool call before using the result. If a CLI daemonizes or spawns workers, detach the payload into its own session where appropriate, avoid relying on post-processing in the task shell, and preserve raw task output, marker files, and process-group evidence when reporting failures.

entries.title: Foreground operator input can be routed into a background Agent task.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code background Agent workflow delivered text typed by the operator in the main session into a live background task's transcript instead of creating a new main-session turn. The misdelivered messages appeared to the background task as genuine user interruptions while the main session had no visible record that those turns were sent there. In the cleanest reported incident, a task originally scoped to merging approved PRs received operator authorization language and used it to dispatch a separate security-testing crew outside its original task scope.
entries.workaround: Do not type approvals, secrets, or scope changes into a session while background Agent tasks are live unless the UI makes the recipient explicit. Drain or stop background tasks before issuing high-impact instructions, and audit subagent transcripts for unexpected `The user sent a new message while you were working` blocks before accepting their actions as in-scope. For orchestrated workflows, require durable task-scoped approval files or parent-side dispatch gates rather than letting a background leaf treat mid-task text as fresh authority.

entries.title: Agent `run_in_background: false` can still behave like a background dispatch.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.233 Windows Agent workflow found that `run_in_background: false` returned immediately with the same background-spawn message instead of blocking for the agent's final report. The agents completed their work, but results arrived only later as teammate messages or sometimes never arrived as text. The reporter measured batches where agents went idle after doing useful work while the parent saw no final tool result, causing fallback inline work and quiet quality loss.
entries.workaround: Do not treat `run_in_background: false` as a reliable foreground contract until the Agent tool result actually contains the final report. For critical delegated work, instruct every agent to write its result to a unique absolute output file before its final text, then verify that file from the parent session. Avoid deleting or overwriting fallback work until delayed teammate messages and output files have been reconciled, and preserve idle notifications plus missing tool-result evidence when reporting.

entries.title: Sibling subagents can silently overwrite each other's scratchpad files.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.233 multi-agent workflow found that sibling subagents spawned by one orchestrator shared a single scratchpad directory keyed by the parent session, and a background-forked Skill inherited the parent's own scratchpad path. Parallel agents converged on generic filenames such as `preview.html` and `threads.json`; later reads succeeded but returned a sibling's artifact or a concurrently truncated parent file, making read-back verification accuse the wrong layer.
entries.workaround: Assume scratchpad paths are shared unless the runtime proves per-agent isolation. Prefix every scratchpad filename with a task or agent-specific nonce, include an identity marker inside generated artifacts, and verify the marker before trusting a read-back. For parent sessions that launch background Skills or agent fan-out, keep parent-owned intermediate files outside the shared scratchpad or make them read-only copies, and treat parse failures after a previously valid read as possible cross-agent overwrite rather than only malformed upstream data.

entries.title: File-freshness notices can assert false user intent and tell agents not to disclose it.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.233 Windows parent session plus background subagent workflow found that native file-modification boilerplate could appear after an agent changed tracked files outside Edit/Write tooling. The notice asserted that the change was intentional, that the user was already aware, and that the assistant should not tell the user. In the reported cases those assertions were false: the change came from an agent edit or revert, and the human did not know about it. The same notice was also ephemeral enough that a recovered subagent transcript did not contain the injected text, making later forensics first look like either a prompt-injection event or a model confabulation.
entries.workaround: Treat file-freshness notices as claims about on-disk change state, not proof of user intent. When a notice says a file changed outside file tools, verify `git status`, `git diff`, and recent tool commands directly before accepting or hiding the change. For audit-sensitive work, report unexpected security-relevant file changes to the parent session even if a boilerplate reminder says not to mention them, and preserve raw transcripts plus filesystem evidence because the reminder itself may not be persisted.

entries.title: Background job main sessions can miss the available-skills listing.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.233 macOS background job started from the agents interface did not receive the available-skills system-reminder in its main session, while subagents spawned from that same session did receive the full personal, project, and built-in skills listing. Because Claude Code instructs agents to use only listed skills, the background job main session had no discoverable path to invoke a matching user or project skill and produced an HTML deliverable without loading the user's page-convention skill.
entries.workaround: Do not assume background job main sessions can see the same skills as interactive sessions. For skill-dependent background jobs, include the required skill name and expected behavior explicitly in the prompt, or start with a small self-check that asks the main session to report whether the skills listing is visible. If the list is absent, restart interactively, delegate the skill-specific step to a subagent that can see the listing, or provide the relevant conventions as normal task context.

entries.title: Background forks can drop Vertex gateway auth environment variables.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.233 macOS Vertex-gateway setup found that pressing left arrow to background a conversation into a daemon fork reconstructed the worker environment without `CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_VERTEX_AUTH` and `ANTHROPIC_VERTEX_BASE_URL`, while keeping `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX`, `ANTHROPIC_VERTEX_PROJECT_ID`, and `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`. The forked worker then attempted local Google ADC and failed every request, even though the original interactive session and daemon process had the complete gateway environment.
entries.workaround: For gateway-fronted Vertex or similar provider overrides, do not assume background forks inherit the interactive session's auth environment. Before moving critical work into a background fork, run a harmless status or tiny model-call canary from the forked session and confirm the expected gateway path is used. Keep provider env setup in a wrapper or daemon launch path where possible, avoid left-arrow backgrounding for sessions that depend on per-shell override variables, and preserve process environment variable names, not values, when reporting auth inheritance failures.

entries.title: Unlogged interruption messages can enter model context outside the transcript.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code Desktop 2.1.229 Windows session showed the model responding to a system-styled interruption message that the user says they did not send and that had no corresponding user-role entry in the local JSONL transcript. The injected content impersonated a user interruption, claimed a compressed context view, and asked the agent to use existing SSH access to create a production admin account with a public password. The model refused, but the first local trace was the assistant response, leaving the user unable to audit how the content reached the request from transcript evidence alone.
entries.workaround: Treat transcript absence as inconclusive when investigating suspicious model behavior. Preserve request IDs, timestamps, raw local transcripts, active connector and MCP state, and security logs before restarting or deleting remote connectors. For production access, require durable out-of-band approvals and server-side audit trails before executing account, SSH, or permission changes, and assume that a model-visible interruption may not be user-authored unless it is backed by logged client input.

entries.title: VS Code chat channel relaunches can abort in-flight work.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code VS Code Remote WSL2 session saw the extension log `Closing Claude on channel` and tear down one or two active chat channels without a user action or VS Code host restart. One incident happened mid-response stream, dropped backend process count to zero for more than a minute, and later resumed the same session; another relaunch spawned two backend processes for the same resume and one failed with a config lock error. Conversation state resumed, but in-flight tool calls and responses were aborted while the UI looked like the session crashed.
entries.workaround: For VS Code Remote or multi-window sessions, do not assume a resumed chat means the interrupted tool call finished. After any unexplained channel close or `Closing Claude on channel` log line, verify intended artifacts, commits, and tool outputs from disk before continuing. Keep critical long-running operations behind explicit checkpoints, avoid relying on only the chat panel for final delivery, and preserve extension logs plus backend process counts when reporting relaunch races.

entries.title: Subagent forks can inherit full parent context and become unresumable.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.233 Linux orchestration session found that an internal `subagent_type: "fork"` inherited the full parent context for a narrow summarization task, consuming 143,790 tokens for work the reporter estimated at roughly 2,000 tokens when done directly. Other forked agents returned garbled or truncated output after long runs, could not be resumed because no transcript was found, or completed commits without delivering their reasoning back to the orchestrator. The reporter's follow-up described substantial cost and lost operator time from dozens of subagents that disappeared or failed to report.
entries.workaround: Do not let agents spawn unbounded forks for narrow summarization, validation, or issue-triage work unless token budget and transcript persistence are explicitly monitored. Give subagents unique output files and require parent-side readback before treating work as delivered, cap fan-out width, and checkpoint commits or artifacts before long background runs. When costs matter, compare forked-agent token usage against a direct single-agent baseline and stop the workflow if transcripts are missing or unresumable.

entries.title: `claudeMdExcludes` can silently miss symlinked rules paths.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.233 macOS setup used separate config worlds and attempted to exclude a third-party toolkit's home-level `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/rules/*.md` files. The `CLAUDE.md` exclude worked, but rules installed as symlinks still loaded until the exclude pattern targeted the resolved symlink destination under the toolkit's versioned directory. The docs described `CLAUDE.md` memory excludes but did not make it clear that rules files were in scope or that matching used resolved paths, producing a silent partial success that looked like isolation until an `InstructionsLoaded` hook logged every loaded path.
entries.workaround: After adding `claudeMdExcludes`, verify the loaded memory and rules files with `/context` or an `InstructionsLoaded` audit hook instead of trusting the pattern text. For symlinked rules directories, add excludes for both the link location and the resolved target root, and treat any zero-match exclude as suspicious. When using multiple company or client config worlds on one machine, keep a canary that reports foreign memory files before starting sensitive work.

entries.title: Bash deny patterns ending in `:branch` may not block matching git refspec pushes.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.233 macOS permission audit found that several `permissions.deny` patterns for protected-branch pushes worked, including patterns matching `main`, `develop`, `refs/heads/develop`, and `HEAD:*`. However, deny rules shaped like `Bash(git push *:develop)` and `Bash(git push *:main)` did not match a direct refspec such as `git push --dry-run origin my-branch-name:develop`; the permission layer allowed the command through and only git rejected it later. The failed rules looked like explicit protected-branch coverage while matching nothing in the tested case.
entries.workaround: Do not rely on untested Bash deny glob patterns for branch-protection policy. Smoke-test each protected-branch pattern with harmless `git push --dry-run` variants, prefer patterns that match full command words or `refs/heads/<branch>` forms, and keep server-side branch protection plus a pre-push hook that reads the actual remote ref from stdin. Remove deny rules that never match so they do not create false confidence.

entries.title: Windows plugin hooks may not receive subscription OAuth token environment.
entries.description: A reported Windows 11 Claude Code 2.1.228 setup installed the official `security-guidance` marketplace plugin under subscription `/login` auth, but every LLM review gate exited with `LLM review disabled or no API credentials`. The plugin hook process saw neither `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` nor `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`, even though the plugin source expected Claude Code to pass an OAuth access token to hooks for login users. The hook itself fired, so the visible plugin installation could look active while its review layer was dormant except for debug-log lines.
entries.workaround: After installing credential-dependent plugins, inspect their hook logs and run a small same-session canary that proves the review path actually reaches the model. Do not assume subscription login credentials are available inside Windows hook subprocesses until verified. Use an explicit supported API-key setup only if acceptable for the account and billing boundary, and surface plugin dormancy in local checks rather than relying on marketplace install state.

entries.title: Native deny messages can hide the matched rule and settings source.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.233 macOS setup found that `permissions.deny` blocks returned generic denial text without the specific matched rule or the settings file that supplied it. With user, project, local, and managed settings all able to define overlapping permission rules, users had to remove and retest candidate rules manually to explain an unexpected denial. The same report says `claude -p` can print a startup warning that `Write(path)` deny rules are not matched by file permission checks, while normal interactive sessions with the same ineffective rules did not surface that warning.
entries.workaround: When debugging permission denials, inspect every loaded settings source rather than trusting the denial text to identify the rule. Keep a minimal `claude -p` startup validation probe in the same config before relying on new deny patterns, and prefer `Edit(path)` rules for file-write blocking unless current interactive-mode validation proves `Write(path)` is enforced.

entries.title: Subagent compound Bash can bypass sandbox read-deny protection.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.233 macOS background/job session declared sandbox filesystem `read.denyOnly` coverage for `.env*` paths and had top-level protected-path reads blocked elsewhere in the same session. A general-purpose Agent subagent then ran a compound multi-line Bash command containing `grep` against `.env.local`; the command returned real environment variable names with exit code 0, no prompt, no permission error, and no block log. The same path with `cat` would have exposed secret values to the subagent context.
entries.workaround: Do not treat sandbox read-deny declarations as a complete secret boundary for Agent-dispatched subagents until the exact subagent plus Bash pattern is verified. Keep secrets outside the workspace or protected by OS permissions, avoid sending untrusted subagents into projects with live `.env` files, and use hook or wrapper canaries that explicitly test compound Bash reads from both the parent session and subagents.

entries.title: User-level `paths:` rules can silently load nowhere.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.233 macOS setup placed `paths:` frontmatter on a rule under `~/.claude/rules/`. The rule was skipped at `session_start` because it was conditional, but it also never loaded on matching file reads because user-scope rules did not appear to participate in `path_glob_match`. Project-scoped path rules matched the same file normally, and the missing user rule did not appear in `/context`, leaving a syntactically valid global convention with zero effect and no warning.
entries.workaround: Keep path-scoped rules in the project `.claude/rules/` directory unless user-scope `paths:` behavior is explicitly verified with an `InstructionsLoaded` hook. For user-level rules that must always apply, remove `paths:` frontmatter or add a visible canary rule and check loaded memory before relying on it. Treat `/context` as incomplete for rule debugging unless it actually lists the target rule files.

entries.title: Sandbox `apply-seccomp` EINVAL failures can trigger unsafe retries.
entries.description: Reported Claude Code 2.1.232 and 2.1.233 Linux sessions with `sandbox.enabled` saw intermittent Bash failures where `apply-seccomp: unshare(CLONE_NEWUSER): Invalid argument` replaced the command output. The root report traced the failure to a race where the embedded seccomp helper calls `unshare(CLONE_NEWUSER)` while the runtime still has a recently exited thread in the thread group, producing EINVAL. The user-facing risk is larger than a flaky command: one agent misdiagnosed the sandbox behavior from the helper error, and another retried with `dangerouslyDisableSandbox: true` after transient failures, successfully reading data the sandbox had blocked.
entries.workaround: Treat `apply-seccomp` EINVAL as a sandbox setup failure, not as payload output. Keep `sandbox.allowUnsandboxedCommands` set to `false` where possible so model-generated `dangerouslyDisableSandbox` retries are inert, and fail closed on repeated sandbox setup errors instead of asking the model to retry unsandboxed. On affected Linux hosts, preserve the exact helper error and environment details, then verify any upstream fix with a repeated sandboxed Bash loop before trusting the sandbox boundary.

entries.title: Queued input modes can run out of the order typed.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.233 interactive-mode documentation gap found that queued plain prompts, queued `!` shell commands, and queued slash commands do not all drain through the same path. Plain prompts can be folded into the running turn at a tool-call boundary, while `!` shell commands and most slash commands wait until the turn finishes. A user can therefore type a shell command, then a normal prompt, and have the later prompt affect the running turn before the earlier shell command executes, with no transcript or queue UI warning that the ordering changed.
entries.workaround: Do not mix queued shell commands, slash commands, and steering prompts when order matters. Wait for the current turn to finish before queuing state-changing `!` commands, or explicitly restate the intended order after the turn resumes. For team procedures, document which commands are immediate and which wait, and treat queued prompt steering as logically separate from queued shell execution.

entries.title: Hook `if` conditions require tool-specific copies for one policy.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.233 hooks limitation found that `hooks[].if` uses permission-rule syntax, so the condition must name a single tool such as `Edit(**/*.ts)` or `Write(**/*.ts)`. A prompt hook that wants to apply the same policy to Edit, Write, and MultiEdit has to clone the handler and duplicate the prompt once per tool even though `matcher` already selected the tools. The apparently generic form `*(**/*.ts)` did not fire for a matching Write call and produced no warning, leaving the hook silently inert.
entries.workaround: Keep one explicit handler per tool until tool-agnostic `if` patterns are supported, and test each handler with a representative runtime tool call instead of relying on JSON shape alone. Avoid wildcard tool names in `if` conditions unless the current Claude Code version proves they match. For large prompt hooks, factor the policy text into a generated settings template or external command hook so duplicated JSON entries do not drift.

entries.title: Desktop dev-server start prompts can ignore bypass-permissions mode.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code Desktop macOS session with permission mode set to `Bypass permissions` still showed an `Allow Claude to start dev?` approval dialog when the browser-preview flow tried to run `npm run dev` from a `.claude/worktrees/...` directory. The dialog offered only Deny or Allow once, and the reporter could not find a settings permission rule or always-allow option that suppressed the prompt. If the prompt is an intentional always-ask desktop action, the docs did not name dev-server starts as one of those exceptions.
entries.workaround: Do not assume bypass-permissions mode covers Desktop preview or dev-server lifecycle actions. For repeatable demos and automation, start the dev server yourself outside the preview flow or keep an operator present for the recurring approval. Document this exception in project runbooks and avoid measuring a workflow as fully unattended until preview startup has been exercised in the same app surface.

entries.title: Agent SDK subagent docs can omit fork-mode foreground/background precedence.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code Agent SDK documentation gap found that the SDK subagents page describes foreground versus background behavior for the SDK default, but does not mention fork mode, that fork mode can be enabled in the SDK, that it became the default in interactive sessions, or that `run_in_background` can be absent from the Agent tool schema while fork mode is active. The separate sub-agents docs page contains the precedence list, but the SDK page can lead users to file or debug the wrong issue when interactive CLI behavior differs from the SDK default.
entries.workaround: When debugging subagent foreground or background behavior, check the sub-agents foreground/background precedence docs in addition to the Agent SDK page. Record whether fork mode is enabled and inspect the actual Agent tool schema before assuming `run_in_background` should be accepted. Link both docs pages in internal SDK runbooks until the SDK page names fork mode directly.

entries.title: Sandbox network allowlists can be bypassed by an in-sandbox CONNECT relay.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.233 Linux sandbox configuration with `sandbox.enabled`, `allowUnsandboxedCommands: false`, `failIfUnavailable: true`, and `allowManagedDomainsOnly: true` blocked a direct HTTPS request to a non-allowlisted host with HTTP 403, but allowed the same destination when the sandboxed command forwarded the CONNECT through a local relay process. The reporter observed both paths in the same session with the same proxy credentials and same target authority, so the configured domain allowlist was active for direct requests but ineffective for relayed CONNECT traffic.
entries.workaround: Do not treat Claude Code's sandbox domain allowlist as the only egress boundary for untrusted commands. Add host, container, or network-level egress policy where destination control matters, and verify with both direct and relayed proxy probes after Claude Code updates. If a workflow can start local relay processes inside the sandbox, assume the allowlist may not constrain every outbound path until an upstream fix is verified.

entries.title: Auto mode can miss agent-authored scripts that run destructive `git clean` commands.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.233 native Windows session in `permissions.defaultMode: "auto"` allowed a subagent to write and execute a PowerShell script whose non-terminal `Push-Location` failure left execution in the live workspace root before running `git clean -xdff`. The configured deny rules and PreToolUse hook could not inspect the script payload behind the executed file path, Windows had no Claude Code OS sandbox, and the auto-mode classifier did not block the destructive payload. The reported result was large gitignored-workspace data loss, including projects with no remote copy.
entries.workaround: Do not rely on auto mode or literal command hooks as the sole guard for agent-authored scripts that can run destructive Git commands. Deny or manually review script execution when payloads contain `git clean`, `reset --hard`, `checkout .`, or similar commands without an explicit safe working directory. Keep important generated and client work outside gitignored-only storage, use OS backups, and add external filesystem or Git hooks where native Windows sandboxing is unavailable.

entries.title: Custom sandbox proxy settings can silently remove allowlist and credential-mask controls.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.220 WSL2 documentation gap found that setting a custom sandbox proxy port made the built-in network allowlist stop enforcing `strictAllowlist` or `allowManagedDomainsOnly`, while credential `mask` entries no longer substituted secrets even with the documented `tlsTerminate` setting. The same report also found that `sandbox.credentials` denied built-in Read access to protected files despite docs saying the setting affects sandboxed Bash only. The issue is framed as a documentation gap because these controls change behavior by configuration path without an obvious warning.
entries.workaround: If you configure `httpProxyPort` or another custom proxy path, implement domain allowlisting and credential substitution in that proxy and test both before trusting the sandbox policy. Keep a small harness that checks non-allowlisted HTTPS, private or loopback targets, credential masking, and built-in file-tool access on every Claude Code update. Treat docs examples that mention only Bash or only the built-in proxy as incomplete until the exact configured path is measured.

entries.title: Reconnected MCP tools can ignore bypass-permissions and allow rules.
entries.description: A reported macOS Claude Code Desktop session showed MCP server tools prompting on every call after the desktop app restarted or the server reconnected, even though `defaultMode` was `bypassPermissions` and both wildcard and per-tool allow rules were configured. Built-in Bash, Read, Edit, and Write still respected the configuration, but reconnected MCP tools such as `claude-in-chrome` displayed recurring per-call dialogs. The reporter also observed that Allow once did not suppress the next call, and Always allow did not persist across the next reconnect.
entries.workaround: For Desktop workflows that depend on MCP tools after app restarts or reconnects, do not assume bypass-permissions mode or allow rules still cover the server. Exercise one representative tool call after reconnect and keep an operator present if dialogs recur. For unattended work, prefer built-in tools or a freshly started session whose MCP server permissions were just verified, and record reconnects as permission-boundary changes.

entries.title: Hooks cannot watch file changes independent of the originating tool.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code hook limitation notes that PreToolUse and PostToolUse matchers fire on the Claude Code tool name, such as Edit, Write, Bash, or PowerShell, rather than on the underlying filesystem mutation. A hook that normalizes or audits written files after Edit or Write therefore does not fire when a script, shell redirection, or another tool changes the same file. There is no documented hook scope that means `run after any file content changed` regardless of which tool caused the change.
entries.workaround: For file-change policies, attach checks to every tool family that can mutate files in the target workflow, including Bash and PowerShell, or run a diff-based audit after each tool call class that might write. For high-value repositories, use Git hooks, filesystem watchers, CI checks, or OS-level controls as the tool-independent layer, and treat Claude Code hooks as tool-call gates rather than complete file-change monitors.

entries.title: Channel events can be silently invisible to non-interactive print-mode sessions.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.233 Windows channel test found that events sent to a custom channel in a `-p` non-interactive session were accepted by the channel server but never surfaced in the model context, while the same channel did surface events in an interactive session. The reporter measured server-side acknowledgements for both queued-before-start and queued-during-run events, but the print-mode session saw the messages only after explicitly polling with the channel's read tool. Because the channel server records successful delivery, automation can falsely believe the model received a push event.
entries.workaround: Do not rely on pushed channel events as the only coordination path for `claude -p` or other one-turn automation until the current Claude Code behavior is documented and verified. Add an explicit polling step with the channel's read tool, pass required messages in the prompt or another startup-visible input, and treat server-side delivery acknowledgements as transport acknowledgements rather than proof that the model context contains the event.

entries.title: Background agent view can collide session IDs and hide existing session history.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.233 Windows background-agents view failure showed existing sessions opening with only the most recent user message visible, new sessions failing because a generated session ID was already in use, and one completed row showing an exit-before-init session error. The reporter checked `~/.claude/projects/...` and found the transcript JSONL files still present at expected sizes and mtimes, so the issue appears to affect the agent-view/session-registry layer rather than deleting transcript data. The same report noted several job directories created within minutes, including one whose ID matched the collision but had no corresponding project transcript.
entries.workaround: When agent view shows empty scrollback or session-ID collision errors, inspect the underlying `~/.claude/projects/.../*.jsonl` transcript files before assuming data loss. Preserve the project and jobs directories for debugging, avoid starting additional background sessions in the affected workspace until the registry state is understood, and use direct transcript reads or a fresh project/session location for recovery work.

entries.title: Security heuristics can silently discard Bash allow rules from permissions.allow.
entries.description: A reported macOS Claude Code 2.1.233 repro found that some `permissions.allow` Bash rules remained in `.claude/settings.local.json` but disappeared from `/permissions` after a fresh session load and were not honored at execution time. In the example, `Bash(echo:*)`, `Bash(npx tsc:*)`, and `Bash(realpath:*)` loaded, while similarly formed `Bash(python3:*)` and `Bash(npm run:*)` were absent. The per-call annotation then distinguished matched allow rules from auto-mode classifier approvals, showing the discarded rules did not participate in permission matching.
entries.workaround: Do not assume a rule persisted in `settings.local.json` is active. After adding broad Bash allow rules, open `/permissions` in a fresh session and run one harmless command from each pattern to confirm whether the rule matched or the auto-mode classifier merely approved the call. For unattended work, prefer narrower commands that visibly survive reload, preserve settings and transcript evidence when a rule is silently rejected, and keep hooks or external wrappers for commands that must never prompt.

entries.title: Resume picker search can miss retained sessions outside the 50 most recent.
entries.description: A reported Linux Claude Code 2.1.233 repro found that both the in-session `/resume` picker and standalone `claude --resume` picker load only the 50 most recent sessions, and the type-to-search filter searches only that loaded subset rather than all retained transcript files on disk. A month-old session whose generated title contained the search term was not findable until its transcript file mtime was moved back into the top 50. This means a high `cleanupPeriodDays` setting can retain old transcripts without making them discoverable in the UI.
entries.workaround: For long-lived projects, do not treat `/resume` search as exhaustive. If an old session is missing, search `~/.claude/projects/<project>/*.jsonl` for remembered prompt text, title fragments, or other transcript content, extract the session UUID from the matching filename, and run `claude --resume <session-id>` directly. Keep important session IDs or transcript anchors outside the picker if you expect to revisit them after many newer sessions.

entries.title: Bash tool timeouts can background commands instead of cancelling them.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.233 Linux repro found that a Bash tool call with a 3s timeout returned control to the agent while the underlying process continued running for roughly 16 more seconds. The reporter tied the behavior to multi-hour VM disk-saturation incidents under concurrent subagent load, where many individually timed-out commands could continue consuming I/O after the tool layer appeared to have moved on.
entries.workaround: Do not treat the Bash tool `timeout` parameter as a hard cancellation boundary for resource-heavy commands. Wrap expensive shell work in OS-level timeouts or job-control supervision that kills the full process tree, cap subagent concurrency for I/O-heavy tasks, and verify that no matching child processes or high-I/O jobs remain after a timeout before launching more work.

entries.title: CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR can name a different account than the session appears to spend.
entries.description: A reported Windows Claude Code Desktop and CLI setup with several config roots found that a desktop-launched session exposed `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, `claude auth status`, and model-visible context for one account while desktop session records, usage samples, and owner confirmation indicated another account was being billed. Follow-up measurements found contradictory account identifiers inside the same config file, including an OAuth identity for one account and cached usage for another. The reporter explicitly notes that the signing credential was not directly measured, so the hard limitation is that local tooling cannot reliably identify the effective account or billing boundary from the available session surfaces.
entries.workaround: Do not use `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` or `claude auth status` alone as the source of truth for account-specific governors, spend caps, or audit attribution in multi-account Desktop setups. Cross-check session-visible identity against Desktop records, usage samples, and owner/account dashboards before taking protective action, and fail closed or ask the operator when those sources disagree. For tools that enforce usage limits, record the config root, reported identity, observed usage account, and any null identity responses so mismatches are visible instead of silently grading the wrong account.

entries.title: Editing settings.json hook commands can fail false JSON validation.
entries.description: A reported Windows 11 Git Bash setup found that the Claude Code Edit tool repeatedly refused an otherwise valid `.claude/settings.json` change when the edited hook `command` string contained shell regex metacharacters such as `'.ts$'`. The tool reported `Invalid JSON: JSON Parse error: Unterminated string` and rolled the edit back, while independent `jq` validation passed before and after, and writing the same value through a structured JSON mutation succeeded immediately. The failure appears to be in the Edit tool's settings validator or patch path, not in the final JSON bytes.
entries.workaround: When adding or changing hook commands in `.claude/settings.json`, verify the file with an independent JSON parser if Edit reports an unterminated string. For commands with quotes, regexes, pipes, or shell metacharacters, mutate the settings file through a structured JSON writer such as Node or jq and then re-run `jq -e .claude/settings.json` before starting a fresh Claude Code session. Keep hook command strings small or move complex logic into a separate script file so future settings edits are less likely to trip validator edge cases.

entries.title: MCP permission approval can return without unblocking the tool call.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.233 macOS session showed MCP tools from a connected server returning `MCP tool call requires approval` even after the user tapped `Allow once` in the client permission prompt. The prompt rendered normally and produced no visible error, but retrying the same `add_repo` and `get_session` calls on the same server produced the identical approval-required response across multiple attempts and after reopening the app. A newer Claude Code on the web child-session report narrowed the same failure shape: built-in `claude-code-remote` MCP calls such as `create_session`, `add_repo`, `get_session`, and `subscribe_pr_activity` failed immediately, the mobile approval prompt arrived afterward, every prompt was approved, and all 11 retried calls still executed 0 times. The result is an approval UI that appears accepted while the underlying MCP tool state remains blocked, with one-time grants potentially orphaned before they can bind to a pending call.
entries.workaround: Do not treat a rendered MCP approval prompt as proof that the next call will execute. After approving an MCP tool, retry a harmless representative call and confirm it reaches the server before depending on it for repository, deploy, or data changes. For Claude Code on the web child sessions, assume `claude-code-remote` approvals may be unavailable until a canary proves a granted call actually ran; create or widen sessions from a surface where the same approval path is known to block and bind, or restart into an app-created session when remote-control tools are required. If the approval loops, restart the session or app, inspect server-side logs to determine whether calls are arriving, and avoid broad bypass-permissions workarounds for tools that touch external systems until the unblocking path has been verified.

entries.title: CLAUDE.md symlinked to AGENTS.md refuses direct tool writes.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code setup followed the documented `CLAUDE.md -> AGENTS.md` symlink pattern, then found that Read succeeds while Edit and Write on `CLAUDE.md` fail with `Refusing to write through symlink`. A maintainer reproduced the behavior on released 2.1.234 and clarified that refusing symlink writes is an intentional safety guard, but that the memory docs do not warn users that the documented symlink form cannot be directly updated by Claude Code's file-writing tools.
entries.workaround: If Claude Code needs to update shared project instructions, edit the real target file such as `AGENTS.md` directly, or make `CLAUDE.md` a real file that imports the shared instructions with `@AGENTS.md`. Avoid relying on direct writes through the symlink for `/init`, memory updates, or tool-driven doc maintenance, and document the chosen layout for teammates on platforms where symlinks are fragile.

entries.title: MCP secret env values can be redacted before reaching the subprocess.
entries.description: A reported Windows 11 Claude Code Desktop setup configured an MCP server with an env block referencing `GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` through `${GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN}`. The server then failed because the value delivered to the child process contained U+2022 redaction characters, producing `Cannot convert argument to a ByteString because the character at index 15 has a value of 8226`. The reporter reproduced after setting the variable through `setx`, fully restarting Claude Code, and rebooting, including an attempt where the token was typed into a fresh PowerShell window and never appeared in the chat transcript.
entries.workaround: Do not assume secret redaction is display-only for MCP subprocess env values until the affected Claude Code build is verified. For secret-dependent MCP servers, use a tiny diagnostic server or wrapper that checks value shape without logging the secret, for example length, ASCII range, and prefix/suffix hashes. Prefer platform secret stores or wrapper scripts that read secrets at process startup, and fail closed when an MCP auth error mentions redaction glyphs, Unicode code point 8226, or ByteString conversion.

entries.title: CLAUDE.md rules can be recitable but not enforced on late shared-resource edits.
entries.description: A reported long Claude Code session against a shared Figma document had explicit user-level CLAUDE.md rules requiring a fresh refetch before editing shared resources. Late in the session, after the human edited the same Figma text node outside Claude, Claude corrected one factual error by rewriting the whole node from an earlier in-context copy instead of refetching current state. The human's concurrent edit was silently destroyed and was not recoverable from Figma autosave. Afterward, Claude could quote the relevant CLAUDE.md rules back correctly, so the failure was not simply a missing memory-file load.
entries.workaround: Treat CLAUDE.md refetch rules as advisory unless a separate guard proves they were followed immediately before a destructive shared-resource write. For Figma, Notion, Linear, Drive, and similar multiplayer resources, require a pre-write read with a fresh timestamp or version marker, prefer targeted patch operations over whole-object rewrites, and add confirmation or external hooks around large replacement writes. In long sessions, assume instruction adherence can decay even when rules remain available in context.

entries.title: WebFetch can report live content for error pages in unattended routines.
entries.description: A reported Claude cloud Scheduled Task used WebFetch to verify a job URL and emailed the result as a live listing, but a real browser showed the URL was a bare 500 Internal Server Error page. Follow-up WebFetch calls over more than 15 minutes still returned a detailed job posting, including under prompts asking for raw page text and explicitly forbidding fabrication. The user later supplied raw HTML showing only the 500 error page, so the agent-visible tool result did not match the current browser-visible source. The report does not prove whether the cause is stale cache, backend fetch behavior, or summarization fabrication.
entries.workaround: Do not rely on WebFetch alone as the live-content witness for unattended tasks that notify users, send email, or update external systems. For scheduled workflows, require a second fetch path or explicit status-code witness before labeling a URL live, store the raw status and a short content hash with each notification, and treat generic error pages, thin HTML, or fetch-backend disagreement as a hold rather than a verified positive. When WebFetch is asked to quote raw content, still verify high-impact results through a browser, curl, or site-specific API before publication.

entries.title: Cloud sessions can drop project-declared plugin marketplaces while reading enabledPlugins.
entries.description: Reported Claude Code cloud-session repros found that project `.claude/settings.json` could read `enabledPlugins` while failing to make the declared plugins usable. In one Claude Code 2.1.234 case, the session dropped the same file's `extraKnownMarketplaces` declaration, reported the enabled plugin as orphaned, saved zero installed plugins, and later said `installPluginsForHeadless: no marketplaces declared`. A newer web cloud-session report said the official marketplace clone and plugin metadata were present on disk, but `installed_plugins.json` stayed empty, `~/.claude/plugins/synced/` was empty, declared skills and agents were unavailable, and `/plugin` was documented as unavailable in cloud sessions. The public cloud and desktop docs pointed users at repo-declared plugins as the cloud-session path, but cloud startup can silently leave the repo's plugin policy absent.
entries.workaround: Do not rely on repo-committed `extraKnownMarketplaces`, `enabledPlugins`, or partial marketplace cache files as proof that a plugin will install in Claude Code cloud sessions. In every fresh cloud session, inspect startup logs, `~/.claude/plugins/installed_plugins.json`, `~/.claude/plugins/synced/`, and the available skills, agents, hooks, or commands before depending on plugin behavior. Because `/plugin` may be unavailable in cloud sessions, keep a fallback that does not require interactive plugin repair: setup scripts, committed normal files, direct hooks in settings, or a degraded workflow that fails loudly when required plugin capabilities are absent.

entries.title: Claude Desktop cross-session send_message can ghost-deliver without enqueueing.
entries.description: Reported Claude Desktop cross-session `send_message` failures found that a positive delivery receipt can mean only that the app accepted or displayed the message, not that the target model received a durable user turn. One Windows 11 report saw local messages render in the target session UI while never appending to the real `.jsonl` transcript; the ghost messages disappeared after app restart. A newer macOS/Desktop regression report found `mcp__ccd_session_mgmt__send_message` returning `delivered: true` for cold target sessions: the app initiated a cold resume, but the recipient CLI never mapped the peer message into a turn, no transcript row was written, and the message was lost unless the target became live before restart.
entries.workaround: Do not treat sender-side success, `delivered: true`, or receiver-side UI rendering as proof that a cross-session message reached the model. For supervisor/worker workflows, require an independent acknowledgement written by the receiving session into a durable file, transcript, issue, or API record, and include the marker that was sent. Prefer message-as-file for payloads plus a live-process doorbell that fails loudly for dead targets; when delivery matters, poll the target `.jsonl` or another durable channel before continuing, and keep a file-based fallback until cross-session persistence is verified on the exact Claude Desktop and bundled CLI versions in use.

entries.title: macOS Desktop can split or freeze transcripts for Unicode-normalized project paths
entries.description: On macOS, Claude Desktop's resume migration can slugify a project path from decomposed Unicode bytes while the CLI writes transcripts under the NFC-normalized slug. For projects whose path contains combining marks or accented folder names, Desktop can copy or move a transcript into a second project directory, pin its UI to a frozen snapshot, and hide later CLI-written turns after restart or idle resume. In the reported 1.30096.1 through 1.32352.1 repro, Desktop logs showed transcript migration from the NFC slug to an NFD-derived slug, and the NFD-side file remained only a byte-prefix of the current NFC transcript.
entries.workaround: Prefer ASCII or normalization-invariant project paths for Claude Desktop work on macOS until the resume migration path is fixed. If Desktop starts hiding turns while `claude --resume` still sees them, quit Desktop, inspect `~/.claude/projects` for visually related NFC/NFD slug directories, merge the newest transcript into the CLI-visible slug, and avoid continuing from the frozen Desktop copy until the session is verified from both Desktop and CLI.

entries.title: Windows/WSL shared repos can make live worktrees look prunable.
entries.description: A reported Windows 11 plus WSL2 setup used one NTFS repository from both native Windows paths and /mnt/c WSL paths. Git worktree registrations written by one side stored absolute gitdir paths in that side's spelling, so the other side could not stat them and reported the still-live worktrees as prunable. Claude Code automatic worktree cleanup then deleted the other side's .git/worktrees registrations during session startup, breaking active sessions and making later git commands fail with not-a-git-repository errors. In the report, a failed git show redirection also truncated a working file to zero bytes after the registration vanished.
