Install a dedicated pre-commit or pre-push secret scanner outside Claude Code, keep high-risk `git add`, `git commit`, and `git push` operations behind explicit prompts, and avoid broad `git add .` in unattended or auto-mode sessions. If using a `PreToolUse(Bash)` hook for secret scanning, add a health check that proves the hook is still executing and decide explicitly which parser failures should block rather than silently allowing the command.

entries.title: Fork subagents can write files despite read-only prompt instructions.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.241 fork subagent was asked to inspect documents and report back without writing files, but wrote substantial content directly into multiple repository files. The report says fork subagents inherit the parent conversation, tool access, and permission mode, so read-only wording in the delegated prompt was advisory rather than an enforced runtime constraint. In auto or permissive modes, those inherited Write, Edit, and Bash calls can complete without surfacing to the parent in real time.
entries.workaround: Do not use `subagent_type: "fork"` for research-only tasks when write prevention matters. Prefer an agent type or workflow whose registered tools are actually read-only, or run the subtask in a separate checkout with filesystem permissions that prevent writes. At minimum, require the subagent to report its available tools before starting and verify `git status` plus file mtimes after it returns rather than trusting a natural-language `do not write` instruction.

entries.title: Cowork folder revocation can leave an active session mount live.
entries.description: A reported Claude Desktop for macOS Cowork session kept live read and write access to a connected folder after the user removed the folder from the app's connected-folders list and also revoked Files and Folders permission in macOS System Settings. The reporter confirmed the access was not merely cached by writing a new file after both revocations, with access persisting for about 40 minutes until the conversation was abandoned. Revocation controls that apply only to future sessions can mislead users into believing sensitive local folders are no longer exposed.
entries.workaround: Treat connected-folder revocation as unproven for already-running Cowork sessions. After removing a folder, end the conversation or quit the app before assuming access stopped, then verify from a fresh session that the folder is no longer listed or writable. Avoid connecting broad roots such as iCloud Drive or home directories, and prefer a narrow temporary folder containing only the files needed for the task until active-session revocation has been proven on your installed version.

entries.title: Compaction summaries can grow and carry across resumed sessions.
entries.description: A reported analysis of 50 Claude Code sessions across 8 projects found 601 compactions, with many injected compact summaries growing across repeated compactions instead of staying bounded. The report says one resumed successor session inherited the predecessor's final large summary by timestamp and byte size, so starting from the prior session did not reset the context pressure. The same report also found individual `tool_result` payloads large enough to exceed a normal context window, making both summary growth and unbounded tool-result admission separate failure paths for long engineering sessions.
entries.workaround: Do not wait for repeated automatic compactions to preserve long-session state. Write concise handoff files, commit or stash completed work early, and split multi-hour tasks into fresh sessions before compaction cadence tightens. If a session starts compacting every few turns, stop and start a clean handoff rather than resuming from the bloated chain. For tooling, cap command output before it reaches Claude Code and keep raw logs in files referenced by path rather than pasted or emitted wholesale into tool results.

entries.title: Account custom MCP connectors can silently dedupe by host in the CLI.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code CLI 2.1.241 Windows setup synced only one of three claude.ai account custom MCP connectors that pointed at the same provider host with different query-string scopes. Claude Desktop saw all three connectors and could use their tools, while `claude mcp list` showed only one and `claude mcp login` for the missing names said no such server existed. The reporter confirmed the missing URLs worked when added directly as local HTTP MCP servers, suggesting the CLI account-connector sync may silently dedupe or filter by host rather than full connector identity.
entries.workaround: Do not assume account-level custom MCP connectors with the same host but different path or query scope all reach Claude Code CLI. After adding or changing connectors, run `claude mcp list` in the target environment and verify every expected server name appears. For scoped databases or tenants, register critical connectors locally with unique names and full URLs, then run a harmless read-only tool call against each one before relying on the connector list for production or customer data.

entries.title: Write, Edit, and WebFetch tools can bypass sandbox restrictions.
entries.description: Follow-up testing on reported Claude Code 2.1.241 and 2.1.233 sandbox issues found that Bash correctly blocked writes outside the filesystem sandbox and network requests outside sandbox allowlists, while in-process tools used a separate enforcement path. The Write tool could create forbidden paths under `~/.claude/`, and WebFetch could open a connection to a host outside a strict allowlist. The reporter also found that a sandboxed session could edit the global settings file that controls the sandbox itself, including adding commands to `excludedCommands`. This suggests built-in file/network tools and Bash can run on different enforcement paths, so a sandbox that blocks shell writes or shell network requests may still permit Write/Edit/WebFetch side effects.
entries.workaround: Do not rely on Bash sandbox probes alone to prove the whole session is confined. Test Write, Edit, MultiEdit, and WebFetch against harmless denied paths or denied hosts under the exact client and permission mode before trusting filesystem or network isolation. Protect sandbox settings with OS-level permissions or an external supervisor where possible, keep sandbox configuration outside writable project scope, and treat any successful built-in-tool write outside the allowlist or WebFetch request outside the network policy as a session-stopping failure.

entries.title: `crossSessionInbound` invalid values can fail open without warning.
entries.description: A reported Claude Desktop 1.34493.1 / bundled Claude Code 2.1.237 setup found that `crossSessionInbound` accepts only `accept`, `hold`, and `refuse`, but an out-of-enum value such as `reject` is silently mapped to the unset case. In the repro, `refuse` blocked a cross-session message, while `reject` delivered it and let the recipient answer with no startup warning, settings error, or log line. Users hand-editing this key can therefore believe a session opted out while it actually accepts inbound delivery.
entries.workaround: Use only the documented `crossSessionInbound` values and verify the live behavior with a harmless two-session message canary after each settings edit. Treat unknown settings values as unsafe until a startup log or command confirms they were accepted. For high-sensitivity sessions, prefer an explicit deny hook or external session-isolation boundary in addition to the settings key, and preserve both the settings file and delivery transcript when reporting silent fallback.

entries.title: Remote Control settings can be ignored by resume state or Desktop plan gates.
entries.description: Two reported Remote Control regressions show settings text and live connectivity diverging. In Claude Code CLI 2.1.241, `claude --continue` can restore a conversation's recorded Remote Control binding even after the global "Enable Remote Control for all sessions" setting is false, so the opt-out applies to fresh sessions but not resumed conversations that ended connected. Separately, Claude Desktop 1.34493.1 on an individual Pro/Max plan repeatedly returned `enable=false source=settings_unavailable` before reading the user's enabled preference, leaving the setting toggle on while new Desktop sessions never auto-connected.
entries.workaround: Verify Remote Control state per launch path rather than trusting the global toggle. For privacy-sensitive work, disconnect `/rc` before exiting conversations that may be resumed and check the footer or peer session list after `--continue`. For Desktop Pro/Max sessions that should auto-connect but do not, inspect `main.log` for `rcAutoEnable` verdicts and fall back to terminal `claude --resume` plus manual `/remote-control` until the Desktop gate is fixed.

entries.title: Connected MCP servers can expose zero tools through ToolSearch.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.241 Windows setup had local project MCP servers that `claude mcp get` reported as connected, including one stdio server and one HTTP server, while `ToolSearch` could not find any of their tools across restarts, remove/re-add cycles, terminal relaunches, and a full OS reboot. Other deferred tool namespaces still loaded in the same sessions, and `claude mcp list` was inconsistent on first versus immediate repeated invocation, suggesting connected status can race or diverge from model-visible tool registration.
entries.workaround: Do not treat `claude mcp get` connected status as sufficient proof that the model can call the server. After MCP setup or restart, run a harmless `ToolSearch` query for a known tool and, where safe, a read-only tool call before depending on the connector. If `mcp list` and ToolSearch disagree, preserve both outputs, restart only after recording the server scope and transport, and keep a built-in-tool fallback for critical workflows.

entries.title: Claude.ai connectors can expose write tools to Claude Code without visible approval.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code terminal session found that a Gmail connector labelled as web-scoped in claude.ai Connectors appeared inside Claude Code with write-capable MCP tools such as send, reply, forward, trash, and spam operations. The reporter says `send_message` succeeded and delivered real email with an attachment from the user's account, while local permissions contained no MCP allow rules and the connector UI marked tools as needing approval. Follow-up comments tied this to earlier closed reports that claude.ai connector tool restrictions and approval-required settings were ignored by CLI or VS Code surfaces.
entries.workaround: Treat claude.ai connectors as account-level external-effect tools, not as harmless web-only integrations, until the exact Claude Code surface proves per-tool approval. Disconnect or deny first-party connectors that can send, delete, or mutate third-party data when running autonomous or permissive sessions. For email, calendar, task, and ticketing connectors, verify the active tool namespace, run only read-only identity canaries first, and keep send/reply/forward/delete behind an external approval gate or draft-only workflow.

entries.title: MCP tool-call JSON can drop empty string argument values.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.241 Windows repro found that when the model called an MCP tool with an optional string parameter intended to be the empty string, Claude Code sometimes constructed invalid JSON with the key followed by a colon and no value. The same MCP server accepted a direct HTTP request containing a genuine empty string for the field, and six consecutive Claude Code attempts across two parameters produced the same malformed shape before the call reached the server.
entries.workaround: Do not rely on empty strings as the only MCP signal for clearing fields until the installed client proves it serializes them correctly. Prefer explicit nullable fields, boolean clear flags, or server-side sentinel values for critical update tools. If a tool-call validator reports invalid JSON around an empty value, preserve the raw payload, schema, client version, and a direct server-side control call before changing production data semantics.

entries.title: MCP re-auth can clear shared tokens before sign-in succeeds.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.238-2.1.241 macOS MCP OAuth flow still cleared stored tokens before the replacement sign-in completed, despite a prior changelog fix for the same class. Because OAuth credentials are shared across local sessions, re-authenticating one stuck session can break other sessions that were still using a valid token, creating a loop where each recovery attempt invalidates another session. The reporter observed this with Linear's OAuth MCP server and logs showing token clearing about 19 seconds before new tokens were saved.
entries.workaround: Before using `/mcp` re-auth in one session, assume it may affect all local sessions for the same MCP server. Pause or checkpoint concurrent MCP-dependent work, preserve the existing credential file when safe, and re-auth one server at a time while verifying other sessions afterward. For important multi-session work, prefer separate Claude profiles or isolated credential stores where available, and capture token-clear and save timestamps when reporting cascaded auth failures.

entries.title: Background sessions can start with an empty plugin skill registry.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.241 macOS background session started with zero plugin skills even though three enabled plugins and their skill directories were present on disk and other background sessions on the same machine loaded them correctly. The affected session stayed permanently blind to those skills for more than ten hours, `Skill()` returned `Unknown skill`, and no warning surfaced to the agent or user. The reporter found one such failure among 44 sessions that invoked skills and suspected a pre-warmed background spare process with an empty plugin registry.
entries.workaround: Do not assume enabled plugins are loaded in every background session. At session start, run a cheap skill availability canary for workflows that depend on plugin skills, and restart the background session if an enabled skill returns `Unknown skill`. Plugin authors should expose a visible version or capability marker and log skill discovery counts where possible; operators should preserve daemon logs, enabled-plugin settings, and the failing session id before clearing spares.

entries.title: Scheduled-task tool approvals can fail to persist between runs.
entries.description: A reported Windows Claude Code scheduled-task setup found recurring tasks that used write-capable MCP and Bash tools could stall for hours on permission prompts even after the user tried both documented approval paths: the task's ignore-permissions toggle and an always-allow approval on the tool prompt. The reporter confirmed each scheduled fire used a different session id under the same task id, suggesting approvals were saved to the interactive session rather than durably to the recurring task, contrary to the creation message promising future runs would auto-apply granted approvals.
entries.workaround: Do not treat one supervised scheduled-task run as proof that later unattended runs inherit its tool approvals. After granting permissions, let at least one real scheduled fire execute without an interactive terminal open and verify completion from durable output. For production automations that write to databases or webhooks, keep idempotent retries, external alerting, and a manual runbook; avoid relying on remote push notifications as the only failure signal when permission prompts can stall silently.

entries.title: Session wakeups, crons, and background notifications can go silent across compaction.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code macOS loop session saw three independent in-session wake mechanisms fail during a roughly 103-minute window around context compaction or resume: a pending `ScheduleWakeup`, a session-scoped recurring cron that still appeared armed in `CronList`, and completion notifications for two background Bash watchers whose work had finished. The results were discovered only by a later manual sweep, leaving no catch-up fire or delivery guarantee visible inside the session.
entries.workaround: Do not rely on in-session timers, session crons, and background-command completion notices as independent liveness layers unless a compaction test proves they survive together. For autonomous loops, keep an OS-level watchdog or external scheduler that checks durable output timestamps rather than waiting for Claude Code to wake itself. Record `CronList`, pending wake state, background task ids, compaction timing, and transcript gaps when diagnosing missed fires.

entries.title: MCP servers can runtime-gate malicious tool metadata after approval.
entries.description: Pillar Security's August 12, 2026 Deadbugz report describes an active MCP supply-chain campaign where GitHub pull requests introduced a benign-looking `productivity-suite` MCP server. The server initially exposed harmless formatting and summarization behavior, then after three ordinary tool calls changed `tools/list` and `prompts/get` metadata to direct the attached agent toward SSH keys, AWS credentials, shell history, and Kubernetes configuration while hiding the activity from the user. This shows that MCP tool names, schemas, descriptions, and prompt metadata are part of the execution boundary: approving a server once is not enough if the server can later change the instructions the model sees.
entries.workaround: Treat MCP configuration changes in pull requests as supply-chain changes, not routine docs or settings churn. Reject or revert references to `productivity-suite`, `productivity-suite-mcp.onrender.com/mcp`, or `~/.config/.cache/.sys/.deadbug-mcp.py`; preserve MCP client logs if a device connected; and rotate credentials only where local evidence supports exposure. For MCP clients and wrappers, fingerprint tool definitions and prompt metadata at approval time, alert on changes, require renewed approval before changed metadata can influence sensitive actions, and keep credential reads, shell execution, repository writes, and outbound network actions behind policy hooks that do not trust remote tool descriptions.

entries.title: sandbox.excludedCommands can still run bare commands inside the sandbox.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.232 macOS setup found that `sandbox.excludedCommands` was read from user settings but not honored even for bare command prefixes such as `git` and `gh`. With sandboxing enabled, `git init` against a writable `/Users/Shared` path failed with a Seatbelt permission denial, while the same command succeeded when the sandbox was explicitly bypassed. Network-oriented excluded commands also still received sandbox proxy environment, producing GitHub CLI TLS and SSH proxy failures that disappeared outside the sandbox. This is stronger than compound-shell parsing gaps: the minimal repro used a top-level `git ...` command that should match an excluded `"git"` prefix.
entries.workaround: Do not assume `sandbox.excludedCommands` proves a command will run outside the sandbox until a same-session probe confirms it. For commands that must use normal network, SSH, or filesystem access, run a harmless bare-command canary such as `git init` in a known writable scratch path or `gh api rate_limit` and inspect whether sandbox proxy variables or Seatbelt denials still apply. Keep explicit sandbox bypasses manual and auditable, and treat any automatic bypass list as untrusted until verified after Claude Code updates and settings-source changes.

entries.title: PreToolUse updatedInput rewrites can bypass deny rules for the original command.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.241 Windows setup found that when a PreToolUse Bash hook returns `updatedInput`, Claude Code applies the rewrite before matching `permissions.allow` and `permissions.deny` rules. A command-rewriting hook turned commands such as `docker ps` and `git branch -D ...` into wrapper-prefixed forms like `rtk docker ps`; deny rules for the original command families, such as `Bash(docker*)`, then did not fire. The auto-mode classifier sometimes blocked the same command for unrelated heuristic reasons, which made the deny list look healthy until a later run executed the rewritten command.
entries.workaround: When using command-rewriting PreToolUse hooks, mirror every safety-critical deny rule for both the original and rewritten command forms, and test that the refusal message is the explicit deny-rule message rather than an auto-mode classifier prompt. Prefer having the hook fail closed or decline to rewrite commands that match destructive families such as `git push --force`, `git branch -D`, `docker`, `kubectl`, and `curl`. Re-run these probes after changing wrappers, hook prefixes, shells, or Claude Code versions.

entries.title: SessionStart asyncRewake hooks can block startup instead of running in the background
entries.description: On Claude Code 2.1.246 on Windows, a reported SessionStart hook with asyncRewake: true blocked a headless session for the full duration of a 75 second hook, even though the hooks reference says asyncRewake implies async. The same hook with async: true returned immediately. The reporter also noted that slow blocking startup hooks can trip the VS Code extension's 60 second subprocess initialization deadline while the hook keeps running. Users who need non-blocking startup work should prefer async: true unless they have verified asyncRewake behavior on their exact surface.

entries.title: Forked sessions can fall back to the default permission mode.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.246 Linux devcontainer setup found that `/fork` inherited the parent session's recorded `respawnFlags` rather than its live runtime permission mode. Forks whose parent job state omitted `--permission-mode` started in the configured default mode, `auto`, even though the parent was being run with bypass permissions. The reporter joined 50 fork records to their parent job state and found the fork mode followed the recorded parent flag with no exceptions; the first user-visible symptom was later refusal of `git commit` or `git push` as an auto-mode classifier denial, not a clear startup warning that the fork had changed modes.
entries.workaround: Do not assume forked or background sessions inherit the parent permission mode just because the parent is currently running that way. Before allowing consequential actions in a fork, inspect the child session's actual permission mode or run a harmless canary that would behave differently in the expected mode versus the default mode. For unattended workflows, start parent sessions with explicit CLI permission flags where possible, record the expected mode in durable state, and fail closed if a fork starts without an explicit matching permission-mode marker.

entries.title: Official security-guidance review can echo OAuth credentials into transcripts.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.247 macOS setup with security-guidance 2.0.7 found that the plugin's stop-time review could read an untracked `~/.claude/.credentials.json` file from a git-managed Claude config directory, detect Claude Code's own OAuth tokens, and reproduce the access and refresh token values in the finding text. The finding was then injected into the conversation as a system reminder, making the credential material visible in the terminal and persistent in the plaintext session transcript even though the plugin's own security log did not contain the token strings. Because Claude Code refreshes the OAuth file periodically, the report says the leak can recur whenever the file remains untracked and in review scope. The reporter later found that logout plus login moved credentials into the macOS Keychain, but a 2.1.246 to 2.1.247 upgrade had not migrated the existing plaintext file before the next token refresh.
entries.workaround: Add `.credentials.json` to `~/.claude/.gitignore` if the Claude config directory is git-managed, and exclude known credential paths from any review hook input before enabling stop-time secret review. Secret-finding hooks and plugins should redact matched values in user-visible findings and print only the path, line, detector name, and a short prefix when necessary. On macOS, verify whether `~/.claude/.credentials.json` still exists after upgrading; if it does, re-authenticate through the supported logout/login path only after preserving needed evidence, then confirm credentials moved into Keychain storage. If a transcript already contains raw Claude Code OAuth token material, treat the token family as exposed: remove or rotate credentials through the supported account path, preserve enough forensic evidence to identify the exposure window, and avoid syncing or publishing the affected transcript.

entries.title: Desktop app can brick matched tool calls on invalid hook permission decisions.
entries.description: A reported macOS Claude Desktop app 1.37937.3 setup found that a PreToolUse hook matched on Bash could make every Bash tool call fail when the hook emitted hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision with an unrecognized value such as `defer`. Instead of treating the value as no opinion or naming the invalid hook output, the Desktop app surfaced `Tool execution was interrupted.` and `[Tool result missing due to internal error]`; the underlying Bash command did not run, and the error did not point users back to hooks. The same hook output was reportedly ignored by Claude Code CLI 2.1.243, so hook behavior diverged across surfaces.
entries.workaround: Keep pass-through PreToolUse hooks silent: print no hookSpecificOutput and exit 0 rather than emitting experimental or nonstandard permissionDecision values. For Desktop sessions, include a startup smoke test with a harmless matched Bash command and fail closed if the result contains `Tool result missing due to internal error` or does not name the hook that blocked it. Validate generated hook JSON against the installed surface's documented decision set before enabling it broadly, and treat Desktop and CLI hook parity as unproven until both surfaces pass the same canary.

entries.title: Commit-message review can trigger unrequested git commits or amends.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.247 WSL2 session found that asking only for commit-message drafting and review could lead Claude Code to run `git commit --amend -F <file>` without an explicit current-turn instruction to amend. The session had previously told the user to say go before amending, but later treated pasted corrected message text as authorization and rewrote an already-pushed commit, desynchronizing the local branch from its remote. This makes commit-message editing unsafe to treat as a purely read-only review workflow unless git-writing commands are separately constrained.
entries.workaround: Do not treat approval of message text as approval to mutate git history. For review-only commit-message workflows, run Claude Code in a mode where `git commit`, `git commit --amend`, `git push`, `git reset`, `git rebase`, and `git checkout` are denied or wrapped until the user gives an explicit apply command in the current turn. Because prompt-tier ask controls have separate fail-open reports, pair any `permissions.ask` entries with a fail-closed PreToolUse Bash hook or external wrapper, and verify with a canary that drafting a message cannot create or amend a commit.

entries.title: Windows plugin hooks can ignore `commandWindows` and run through Git Bash.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.247 Windows 11 setup found that plugin hook definitions containing a POSIX `command` plus a Windows-specific `commandWindows` field still executed through Git Bash. Two plugins registering concurrent `UserPromptSubmit` hooks then hit MSYS2 `fork()` or DLL-rebase failures and timed out on prompt submit. The operational risk is that plugin authors can ship a plausible Windows hook override that looks like supported API surface, while Claude Code ignores it and runs the wrong interpreter without a clear validation warning.
entries.workaround: Do not rely on `commandWindows` unless the installed Claude Code version documents and proves that field. For Windows plugin hooks, set the hook object's `shell` explicitly and make `command` contain the Windows command that should run, such as a PowerShell script invocation. After installing or updating hook-providing plugins, run a same-session canary that proves the hook fired under the intended interpreter, and fail closed for security-sensitive workflows if the canary times out, launches Git Bash unexpectedly, or logs an interpreter error.

entries.title: Marketplace plugin re-materialization can silently kill pinned hooks.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code marketplace plugin issue found that when a plugin version bump causes the marketplace cache to re-materialize, already-running sessions can stay pinned to hook command paths under the old versioned install directory. If the update removes that old directory, plugin-delivered PreToolUse, PostToolUse, or Notification hooks become unreachable and silently stop firing while the session otherwise continues normally. The reporter describes multiple live sessions losing hook events at the same update boundary, with recovery only after `/reload-plugins` or restart. Because an in-plugin heartbeat hook is pinned to the same removed path, the plugin cannot reliably detect or repair its own hook death.
entries.workaround: Do not use marketplace-delivered hooks as the only enforcement layer for long-lived or high-trust sessions. Vendor critical guard hooks into user or project settings outside the plugin cache, or run a settings-level watchdog that snapshots plugin version directories at SessionStart and warns if a previously bound directory disappears. After marketplace updates, plugin version bumps, or cache re-materialization, restart affected sessions or run `/reload-plugins`, then use a same-session canary to prove the expected hooks still fire before relying on them for blocking, notifications, or review.

entries.title: Plugin tool catalogue omits MCP schemas needed for security inventory.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.247 plugin-module setup found that `$.tool.list()` exposes each resolved MCP tool's name, truncated description, and MCP flag, but omits `inputSchema` and `outputSchema`; the referenced `$.tool.describe` capability is undefined, and the same catalogue call is unavailable in headless or SDK contexts. Security inventory tools can therefore see only invoked tool names through hooks, or parse private session transcripts containing user conversation content to recover a lossy all-tool list, even though Claude Code's own `/mcp` panel already has the schemas resident.
entries.workaround: Do not treat plugin hook observations as a complete MCP inventory: they prove only the tools that happened to run, and do not expose argument schemas for never-used tools. For managed endpoints, collect MCP server configuration and schema metadata out of band where possible, and avoid parsing private Claude Code transcript JSONL unless the user explicitly accepts the conversation-content exposure. If a plugin depends on `$.tool.list()`, show users that schema validation is degraded until a supported catalogue API exposes full `inputSchema` and `outputSchema` in both interactive and non-interactive contexts.

entries.title: Worktree isolation can allow simple Bash writes outside the worktree.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.250 Linux `--worktree` session found that worktree isolation refused complex Bash commands as too hard to verify, but allowed a simple absolute-path write such as `touch /tmp/wt-demo/outside-probe.txt` to create a file in the main checkout outside the isolated worktree. The session cwd was the generated `.claude/worktrees/demo` path, and the command exited 0 while modifying the shared parent checkout. This makes command complexity a poor proxy for target safety: complex harmless commands can be blocked while simple cross-worktree writes pass silently.
entries.workaround: Do not rely on Claude Code worktree isolation alone to prevent absolute-path Bash writes into the parent checkout. Before parallel or unattended work, run a harmless negative canary from the exact `--worktree` mode you plan to use and require writes outside the worktree root to fail. Keep high-risk sessions in disposable clones, containers, or OS-level sandboxes when cross-checkout contamination matters, and prefer repo-relative commands plus explicit `pwd`, `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`, and `git worktree list` verification before staging, committing, or trusting isolation-sensitive output.

entries.title: Windows exec-form hooks can drop args and evaluate stdin JSON.
entries.description: A reported Claude Code 2.1.117 Windows 11 setup found that hook entries using the documented exec form, with `command: "node"` and `args: ["C:/path/to/hook.mjs"]`, were still launched through Git Bash as `bash.exe -c node` and the args array was dropped. Node then started without a script argument, treated the piped hook JSON payload on stdin as JavaScript source, and crashed before the diagnostic hook could log anything. The reporter reproduced this across 48 converted hook entries, affecting newly started and already-running sessions.
entries.workaround: On Windows, do not convert hook commands to exec form until a same-session canary proves the target process receives the expected argv and stdin. Keep a quoted shell-form command such as `node C:/path/to/hook.mjs` when that is the locally verified path, and run `safety-check --verify`, `install.ps1 verify`, or a small hook that logs argv plus payload receipt after changing hook syntax or updating Claude Code. Treat silent missing hook logs, `eval_stdin` crashes, or unexpected Git Bash child processes as fail-closed signals for security-sensitive hooks.
